title: What's the best "all-in-one" AI for an RPG life-sim game?
author: Tasty-Window
selftext:
I'm looking for one decent all-in-one AI setup (or the closest thing to it) that can actually help across the whole thing brainstorming mechanics and systems, figuring out progression, writing dialogue and character relationships, giving asset direction, and jumping in on the code/scripting side, especially the more complex interconnected parts and NPC stuff.

I don't want to bounce between ten different tools. I'm hoping for one solid platform or workflow that other solo indie devs have actually had luck with on this kind of game (Claude Projects, Cursor combos, whatever).

If you've found something that works well, I'd really like to hear the honest take: pros/cons, what it costs, how good it is at remembering long project context, and any real results from people making similar RPGs.

Thanks!

Tl;dr: whats the most all-in-one (idea to app store) AI platform out there?

comments.author: Dan_Fury
comments.body:
I use Claude Cowork to make games. It can plan and code and since you specify which folder it works on it seems to stay on topic and works quite well. I also regularly update the GDD we wrote together so it can easily look up the current plan and the codebase. It also writes decent stories and character sheets, but honestly that's the part I don't want the ai to do. I did let it write most of the fluff text in the GDD though and that turned out quite well. It feels like letting it write those fluff texts made the ai stay more on topic of my game in general.

The only thing that pisses me off is that Dispatch doesn't work as intended because it doesn't work with a single instance of Cowork and hallucinates bs into the project. I hope they improve it soon, because I can't be the only one that realizes how bad Dispatch is.l in its current form.

replies.author: Dan_Fury
replies.body:
Claude Cowork is in the Desktop app and more like a chat with extended planning mode. It could directly launch your html games and can display md files (basically text documents for your design docs that the ai can easily access). This way you can easily manage the game creation within one tool.
I use Godot and GoPeak as the MCP. Basically  The desktop app allows "plugins" like GoPeak to communicate with other tools like game engines or 3d model software etc.

So if you make a browser game you can test it within Cowork directly and if it is a more complicated 3d game you test it in Godot or your engine of choice

replies.author: solace_01
replies.body:
ok. real advice: download Godot and create a project directory. use claude code (the CLI tool you mentioned) and open it in that directory. read the Godot docs (or send them to AI and ask questions) and go from there

you still have to be the architect and guide the AI in its current state, but claude code is quite capable. there is also Godot MCP so claude can interact directly with Godot

fair warning, $20 plan is fairly limited usage: stick with sonnet instead of opus, start new sessions often to save on token usage, etc. use perplexity to ask questions to learn about Godot or whatever else you need (free web search AI - unlimited)

they key is to learn as you go from the AI. build a lot of prototypes. AI is a skill *accelerator* - and it helps a lot if you build the skills to be accelerated

replies.author: Tasty-Window

replies.author: Living-in-1984
replies.body:
This is GREAT advice - and once you wrap your head around that a bit, look into an 'agent orchestrator' like 'paperclip' or similar if you are ready to run multiple agents simultaneously in a single window.

Level 1: copy/paste code into a chatbot and work with the results (you could skip this, agentic coder didn't exist when I started with AI. This is where most of us started coding with AI)
Level 2: use claude code/codex on your project
Level 3: run multiple instances of claude code/codex simultaneously to get more work done faster
Level 4: too many claude code instances become too unwieldy and you should use an agent orchestrator to manage most aspects of your project if you want to iterate faster

What do I know?
I currently develop software as my day job (*not* at a game studio) in a small team and I build games in my spare time. (Have been coding >20 years hobbyist, >5 years professional)

replies.author: Tasty-Window
replies.body: How do I make sure I don’t loose story elements ? Cause it’s Claude code it will keep the context / GDD files in its window?

replies.author: Living-in-1984
replies.body:
Claude:

"Context retention isn't a tooling problem — it's a project structure problem. Keep your GDD/story files modular (separate docs for lore, characters, quests, etc.) and version-controlled. Feed the relevant files into context per session rather than relying on the AI to "remember" anything. It doesn't. Your job is being the continuity checker — review output regularly, catch contradictions early, and keep your source-of-truth docs clean. No tool or orchestrator fixes a messy project structure."

Me:

One solution that helps greatly (maybe not the most efficient with tokens, but it can help) is having a root CLAUDE.md that is a tree file referencing many other md files where each one covers an individual part of your project. This could be used for any aspect of the project. Be aware that people have mixed opinions on this method.

A 5x max account is the minimum to do what I'm recommending, I smash my limits regularly with a 5x but my 20x work account rarely hits its limits

I hope this helps.

CLAUDE.md (root — references all below)
├── docs/story/lore.md
├── docs/story/characters.md
├── docs/story/quests.md
├── docs/systems/combat.md
├── docs/systems

Then theoretically it only pulls the relative context into memory since claude.md is read on the initial prompt, and will include the other files as it determines the prompt is related to it.

replies.author: Drastykk
replies.body: What have you used for assets generation?

replies.author: Objective-Address810
replies.body:
Good question. 

Opus for base content - lore, world design, narrative hooks, etc.

But that information mostly gets interpreted via different models in game actions - for example Gemini flash or DeepSeek 3.2, but it can and will change over time as models evolve and my gameplay options expand.

Image gen currently mostly Nano Banana. Very good at detail and specifics comparatively.

Random tools for video conversions nothing locked in yet, but not a major focus currently - although it will become a bigger focus.

comments.author: Practical-Frosting81
comments.body: Codex for code. Claude for planning and automating. Frame with codex first and build. Claude can give codex a break, but I used Warp and then Codex refactored  3k lines so the trust is in Codex. Claude does seem pretty good though.  You'll need both if you really start to get in to it. Since RO is for the most part open source you can have ALOT of fun with the AI tools :D
